verdict_blocks.x: Verdict: marginal-thin on these assumptions. A booking conversation costs about 423 toman (about $0.0016) including two SMS messages, and gross margin is 74–82% [D]; the plans charge 1,333–2,000 toman per booking against about 9,535 toman of receptionist time at the minimum wage [D], and about 1.6% of a general practitioner's visit tariff of 126,000 toman [D, S below]. Revenue per customer is only about 1.445M toman a month ($5.45) against 417.1M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 301 paying clinics on paper and 514 with the node and hires counted [D]. The base case (250 customers at month 12, 800 at month 24) breaks even in month 18, with a peak cash need of 4,231M toman (about $15,947) and only +64M a month at month 24 (cumulative cash −4,120M); the conservative case (100 / 300) does not break even (−185M a month, cumulative cash −7,002M); the optimistic case (700 / 2,500) breaks even in month 10 with +940M at month 24. Doubling the GPU price, cutting prices 30% or halving customers each remove break-even. Onboarding and support are the heavy cost: one customer-success hire per 60 clinics costs 42.6% of revenue per customer [D]. Booking marketplaces already list doctors, I found no price for them, and I found no rule on handling patient data. Customer counts are hypotheses [A]. Tags: [S] sourced, [D] derived and recomputed by code, [A] assumption.

r: (a) Doctors with private offices who answer booking calls through a secretary or not at all — core by count. (b) Clinics and polyclinics with a reception desk and several doctors — core by revenue. (c) Dental, physiotherapy and similar practices. Not targeted: public hospitals with state booking systems. Pool: about 100,000 doctors in Iran in a 2011 table [S, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare\_in\_Iran, read 25 Oct 2026; the table gives no source]; in Mashhad 2,915 physicians, about 45% of those registered with the council, had private offices in October 2013, 51.9% general practitioners [S, jmmc.mums.ac.ir/article\_2284, read 25 Oct 2026]. Applying 45% to 100,000 gives about 45,000 doctors with private offices [D, rough: one city, 2013, and doctors have since emigrated or stopped practising; the Medical Council head said about 30,000 general practitioners were unwilling to practise over low fees, 9 Jan 2025 [S, iranintl.com/en/202501093061, read 25 Oct 2026]].

Patients message a Telegram, Bale or Eitaa bot, a web chat or a link on the clinic's page; the bot asks the intake questions the doctor needs (reason, duration, medicines, allergies, insurance), proposes free slots, books, sends the confirmation and reminder by SMS, and hands the doctor a one-paragraph summary before the visit; it does not give medical advice and routes red-flag answers to a human. The labour replaced is the secretary's phone and message time: 4 minutes per booking [A], about 9,535 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance [D]); the plans below charge 1,333–2,000 toman per booking, 14–21% of that [D]. For scale, the tariff for a general practitioner visit is 1.26 million rials (126,000 toman) and for a specialist 1.89 million rials (189,000 toman) [S, iranintl.com/en/202501093061, 9 Jan 2025; the year the tariff was set is not stated].

Direct sales and field visits to clinics in the biggest cities; partnerships with clinic-software and medical-association vendors; referral from medical-supplier representatives; a free booking page for each doctor.

Free pilot of 20 bookings [A]; setup call to load schedules and rules; weekly digest of no-shows and booked slots; one customer-success person per 60 customers [A] (onboarding is heavy). Monthly plan billed in toman, indexed to the exchange rate.

Monthly by number of bookings: Doctor office 600,000 toman for 300 bookings (about $2.26), Clinic 2,500,000 for 1,500 (about $9.42), Polyclinic 8,000,000 for 6,000 (about $30.16) [A, no competitor price was found]. Mix 70% / 25% / 5% [A] gives ARPU 1,445,000 toman a month (about $5.45) [D].

A scheduling engine with clinic rules; Persian intake question sets per specialty reviewed by a physician (clinical content, to be written); an 8B-class open instruction model with Persian capability; a domestic GPU node (RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, Sindad plan 150M toman a month [S]) and SMS access through a domestic provider; 2 engineers, 1 field onboarding hire (40M gross [A]) and 1 customer-success hire.

Loading doctors' schedules and rules; maintaining intake question sets; handling reschedules and cancellations; sending reminders; escalating red-flag answers; monitoring no-show and booking data for each clinic.

Domestic GPU/cloud host; an SMS provider (domestic SMS is about 100–200 rials on the same network and 150–250 rials across networks [S, sent.dm, 3 May 2025]); payment gateway (Zarinpal and similar, worst-case 1% fee [S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%]); a physician adviser for intake questions; clinic-software vendors.

Fixed: team 209.1M toman a month (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-success at 30M + 1 field onboarding at 40M gross [A] × 1.23 [S]), GPU node 150M, other infrastructure 10M, accounting 8M, marketing 40M = 417.1M toman a month (about $1,572) [D]; one-time setup 120M [A] (intake sets and clinic pilots). Variable: gateway 1% of revenue, 60 toman per booking for SMS and handling [A], an extra customer-success hire per 60 customers [A], an extra GPU node when load passes one node's capacity.
[D] (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-success at 30M + 1 field onboarding at 40M gross, salaries [A]) × 1.23 employer insurance [S]
[S] Sindad GPU inference plan, listed 14 Sep 2026
[A] about 3,500 input (about 8 turns with accumulated context) plus about 500 output (replies and the intake summary)
[D] 2,658.57 [S, A6000 vLLM benchmark, Llama-3.1-8B, 100 concurrent] × 0.8 (Ada vs A6000 and Persian token overhead, [A]) × 30% average utilisation [A]
[A] two SMS at 25 toman each (250 rials, upper end of the sent.dm range [S]) plus 10 for handling
[D] 80% use [A] of the 300 / 1,500 / 6,000 quotas, weighted by plan mix

cost_model.x: One node covers about 568 customers at this usage [D: 413,461 ÷ (708 + 20 free-pilot bookings)], so one node is enough in the conservative case, the base case needs a second node at month 24 and the optimistic case needs 5 [D]. Customer-success staffing at one hire per 60 customers costs 615,000 toman a month per customer [D: 36.9M ÷ 60], 42.6% of revenue per customer, the largest cost per customer; if clinics need less hand-holding than assumed this falls, and if they need more break-even moves out. No intake-accuracy or no-show-reduction benefit is priced in.

revenue.x: Break-even is about 301 paying customers on the fixed-cost formula [D: 417.1M ÷ (1,445,000 × 0.99 − 708 × 60) = 300.5], and stepping through customer counts with the node and hires each needs gives 514 customers [D]. Customers ramp linearly from month 4 to the month-12 figure, then to the month-24 figure; the 120M setup falls in month 1.

Customer counts are [A]. For scale only, 800 customers is 1.8% of the rough pool of 45,000 doctors with private offices [D, above], and 2,500 is 5.6% [D]; many customers would be multi-doctor clinics, so the share of doctors reached is higher. In the conservative case cash is still falling at month 24, so the peak cash need is the month-24 position [D]. Cumulative cash at month 24 is −7,002M toman in the conservative case, −4,120M in the base case and +4,098M in the optimistic case [D]; the base-case peak of 4,231M came earlier, and base-case payback is beyond month 24.

sensitivities.x: The base case earns only +64M a month at month 24, so any of the three shocks removes break-even; the low revenue per clinic ($5.45 a month) means fixed cost is covered only at several hundred accounts. Churn is not in the cash rows (the customer path is fixed). At 4% monthly churn [A, clinics keep a booking tool once schedules are loaded, but small offices stop paying] lifetime value per customer is about 34.7M toman [D: (1,445,000 × 0.99 − 708 × 60) ÷ 0.04], and holding 800 customers needs about 32 new customers a month [D: 800 × 0.04]. Marketing cost per customer was not modelled separately; measure it in a pilot.

risks.x: Existing booking platforms: online doctor-booking apps and websites already exist in Iran (Paziresh24 appears as an app listing in search results, and one search headline ranks online doctor-visit searches; pages not opened); I found no price or fee, so the price assumption could be above or below what doctors already pay.
Patient data: intake answers are health data; I found no rule on handling it, but clinics are likely to require domestic hosting and secrecy [A].
Clinical safety: a bot that mis-triages a red-flag answer creates liability; the service must not advise, must escalate, and needs physician-reviewed question sets.

Doctor supply: doctors are emigrating or leaving practice (the Medical Council head cited about 30,000 unwilling general practitioners [S, iranintl.com/en/202501093061]), which shrinks the pool and changes who buys.

Messaging channel access: patients mostly book by phone; adoption of Bale, Telegram and Eitaa bots, and the SMS route, depend on the same platforms and operator rules as #10, and near-total internet blackouts have occurred (Bale, TechRadar, June 2025, as noted in #19).
Onboarding cost: schedules, rules and staff habits differ for every clinic; if onboarding takes more than one customer-success hire per 60 clinics the margin disappears.
Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 [D]).

unverified.x: A current count of doctors with private offices and of clinics (the 100,000 figure is from a 2011 table, the 45% share from one city in 2013).
Prices and fees of Paziresh24 and other booking platforms (Paziresh24's app page is blocked from fetching; search returned titles only).
Rules on handling patient data and on automated intake in private practice.
No-show rates and the real share of bookings made by phone.
Accuracy of an 8B-class open model on Persian medical intake, real tokens per booking, and SMS price under a signed contract.
Zarinpal fee and VAT, as in #1.
Check run: all [D] figures above were recomputed by running the model in code on 25 Oct 2026.

verdict_blocks.x: Verdict: viable on the numbers, but it rests on Persian medical speech recognition that I could not verify. A visit note costs about 856 toman (about $0.0032) including GPU time and audio storage, and gross margin is 76–82% [D]; the plans charge 3,000–4,000 toman per note against about 9,535 toman of typing time at the minimum wage [D], which understates a doctor's time. Revenue per customer is about 2.99M toman a month ($11.27) against 407.1M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 138 paying accounts on paper and 164 with the node and hires counted [D]. The base case (150 accounts at month 12, 600 at month 24) breaks even in month 13, with a peak cash need of 2,711M toman (about $10,219) and +691M a month at month 24 (cumulative cash +1,643M); the conservative case (50 / 200) breaks even in month 22 with a peak cash need of 5,050M and +71M at month 24; the optimistic case (400 / 1,500) breaks even in month 7 with +2,189M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 18, cutting prices 30% to month 19 and halving customers to month 17. The decisive risk is accuracy: on the one public Persian ASR leaderboard I read, a general open model made 36–76% word errors and a fine-tuned Persian model 11–22% on general test sets, and I found no medical-vocabulary test or confirmed licence for that fine-tuned model. Customer counts are hypotheses [A]. Tags: [S] sourced, [D] derived and recomputed by code, [A] assumption.

r: (a) Doctors in private practice who type or hand-write a note for every visit — core. (b) Clinics and polyclinics that equip several doctors. (c) Hospital departments and teaching clinics. Not targeted: hospitals with an in-house record system that forbids add-ons. Pool: about 45,000 doctors with private offices, a rough figure derived in #41 from a 2011 count of about 100,000 doctors and a 45% private-office share in one city in 2013 [D from S, see #41]; the Medical Council head said about 30,000 general practitioners were unwilling to practise over low fees (iranintl.com/en/202501093061, 9 Jan 2025 [S]). At 600 accounts in the base case the mix gives about 1,770 doctor users (420 single doctors, 150 clinics of 5, 30 departments of 20) [D], 3.9% of that pool [D].

The doctor speaks the visit summary in Persian (with drug names, English terms and numbers); the tool transcribes it and fills a structured note: complaint, history, findings, diagnosis, prescription list, advice and follow-up, in the clinic's template, ready to paste into the record or print. The labour replaced is typing: 4 minutes per note [A], about 9,535 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance [D]), far below a doctor's own time value; the plans below charge 3,000–4,000 toman per note, 32–42% of that [D]. Foreign anchors: AI scribes list at $39–$119 per clinician per month for Freed, about $150 for Heidi's paid plan and about $200–$600 for Abridge, and AWS HealthScribe is $0.10 per audio minute [S, getfreed.ai/resources/cost-of-ai-scribes, dated 21 Jul 2026, read 25 Oct 2026; vendor-comparison page, not independently verified]; the Doctor plan below at about $4.52 a month is 3.8–11.6% of Freed's range [D], and a 3-minute note at the AWS rate is $0.30 against about $0.015 here [D].
Phone and web app with one-tap recording; clinic-software integrations; sales through medical societies and supplier representatives; a free trial to individual doctors who then bring their clinics.

Free first 20 notes [A]; custom note templates per specialty and per doctor; correction learning (the tool remembers drug lists and phrasing the doctor edits); one customer-success person per 60 accounts [A]. Monthly plan billed in toman, indexed to the exchange rate.

Monthly by number of notes: Doctor 1,200,000 toman for 300 notes (about $4.52), Clinic 5,000,000 for 1,500 across 5 doctors (about $18.85), Department 18,000,000 for 6,000 across 20 doctors (about $67.85) [A, no Iranian competitor price was found]. Mix 70% / 25% / 5% [A] gives ARPU 2,990,000 toman a month (about $11.27) [D].

A Persian speech-recognition model that handles medical terms, drug names and mixed Persian-English speech (an open Persian fine-tune such as gooya-v1.4 scored 11–22% word error on public test sets [S, navidved Open Persian ASR Leaderboard, 23 Oct 2026]; its licence was not confirmed); a note-structuring 8B-class instruction model; a medical term and drug list; a domestic GPU node (RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, Sindad plan 150M toman a month [S]); 2 engineers, 1 clinical language editor (40M gross [A]) and 1 customer-success hire.

Transcribing and structuring notes; building medical vocabulary and template sets; measuring word and field error rates with doctor-corrected samples; integrating with record or clinic software; keeping audio and notes secure.
Domestic GPU/cloud host; payment gateway (Zarinpal and similar, worst-case 1% fee [S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%]); a physician adviser; clinic-software vendors; medical societies as channels.

Fixed: team 209.1M toman a month (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-success at 30M + 1 clinical editor at 40M gross [A] × 1.23 [S]), GPU node 150M, other infrastructure 10M, accounting 8M, marketing 30M = 407.1M toman a month (about $1,535) [D]; one-time setup 150M [A] (vocabulary, templates and doctor-reviewed test sets). Accounts ramp linearly from month 4 to the month-12 figure, then to the month-24 figure; the 150M setup falls in month 1.

Account counts are [A]. At month 24 the base case is about 1,770 doctor users, 3.9% of the rough 45,000 private-office pool [D, above]; the optimistic case is about 4,425 users, 9.8% [D: 1,050 single doctors + 375 clinics × 5 + 75 departments × 20], and the conservative case about 590 users [D]. Cumulative cash at month 24 is −4,909M toman in the conservative case (payback beyond month 24, so the peak cash need of 5,050M came earlier), +1,643M in the base case and +16,531M in the optimistic case [D].

sensitivities.x: No single stress removes break-even in the base case, but each leaves it thin, and a 30% price cut together with the unmeasured speech speed would erase most of the month-24 profit. Churn is not in the cash rows (the customer path is fixed). At 5% monthly churn [A, doctors stop dictating if corrections take longer than typing] lifetime value per account is about 58.9M toman [D: (2,990,000 × 0.99 − 708 × 20) ÷ 0.05], and holding 600 accounts needs about 30 new accounts a month [D: 600 × 0.05]. Marketing cost per account was not modelled separately; measure it in a pilot.

risks.x: Medical-term accuracy: general Persian ASR is poor on specialised speech (whisper-large-v3 scored 36–76% word error on the leaderboard's four test sets, 75.7% on customer-service calls; a fine-tuned Persian model 11–22% [S, navidved leaderboard, 23 Oct 2026]); drug names, Latin terms and numbers are the hard part and no medical test set was found. A wrong dose in a note is a safety issue, so the doctor must review every note.
Licence of the Persian ASR model: not confirmed (as in #17); a non-commercial licence would block the service until a model is built or licensed.
Patient data: voice and notes are health data; I found no specific rule, but clinics are likely to require domestic hosting and secrecy [A].
Integration: notes are only useful if they reach the clinic's record or print template; Iranian clinic software varies and I found no integration standard.
Habit: doctors who already type quickly or use paper may not adopt dictation, and clinic noise degrades audio.
Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 [D]).

unverified.x: Persian ASR word error on medical speech and the licence of any open model that reaches it.
Any Iranian price for dictation, transcription or clinic-software modules.
The number of doctors who type notes for every visit, and a current count of private-office doctors.
Rules on storing and processing patient voice and records.
Real speech-recognition speed on Persian clinic audio (30 times real time is an assumption derived from an English-pipeline benchmark).
Zarinpal fee and VAT, as in #1.

verdict_blocks.x: Verdict: viable on the numbers in the base case, but thin in the conservative case and blocked by two things I could not verify: a Persian-population-validated image model and the medical-device rules for diagnostic software. A scan costs about 2,886 toman (about $0.0109) to analyse, including GPU time and a 3% specialist audit, and gross margin is 68–84% by plan [D]; the plans charge 7,500–15,000 toman per scan against about 19,070 toman of specialist reading time at the minimum wage [D], which understates a specialist's time. Revenue per account is about 5.55M toman a month ($20.92) against 510.5M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 118 paying accounts on paper and 135 with the node and hires counted [D]. The base case (120 accounts at month 12, 450 at month 24) breaks even in month 13, with a peak cash need of 3,921M toman (about $14,779) and +1,186M a month at month 24 (cumulative cash +3,536M); the conservative case (40 / 150) breaks even in month 23 with a peak cash need of 6,983M and only +67M at month 24, and it has not paid back by month 24; the optimistic case (300 / 1,200) breaks even in month 8 with +3,815M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 14, cutting prices 30% to month 17 and halving customers to month 18. The decisive risks are clinical: I found no public accuracy figure for an image model on Iranian clinics' panoramic and chest films, and no Iranian rule on diagnostic AI, so the tool must be sold as a second reader whose findings a clinician confirms, and a licence for any open medical-image model is unconfirmed. Customer counts are hypotheses [A]. Tags: [S] sourced, [D] derived and recomputed by code, [A] assumption.

r: (a) Dental offices that take panoramic, bitewing and periapical films — core. (b) Radiology clinics that read chest, spine and dental films for referrers. (c) Dental or hospital chains and hospital radiology departments. Not targeted: patients directly. Pool for (a): Iran had 35,404 dentists in 2019 (30,811 general, 4,593 specialists), 43 per 100,000 people (Journal of Oral Health and Oral Epidemiology, johoe.kmu.ac.ir/article\_91637.html, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]); with 60% of them in private offices [A, no source found] that is about 21,242 offices or practitioners [D], and the base case at month 24 (450 accounts, about 360 of them dental offices) is 2.1% of that pool [D]. I found no count of Iranian radiology clinics.

The tool reads an uploaded panoramic or chest film, marks suspected findings (caries, periapical lesions, bone loss, impacted teeth, nodules or fractures on the chest or limb films) and drafts a one-paragraph note, so the dentist or radiologist reviews a prepared reading rather than starting from nothing. The labour replaced is the first read: 8 minutes per film [A], about 19,070 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance [D]); the plans charge 7,500–15,000 toman per scan, 39–79% of that [D]. Foreign anchors: dental-AI subscriptions cost roughly $200–$500 a month per office, average $300, and consumer apps $5–$25 per scan [S, realdentalcosts.com/en/dental-costs/ai-dentistry-diagnosis-cost, reviewed 31 May 2026, read 26 Oct 2026; US edition, from vendor and practice data, not independently verified]; the Overjet comparison page says Overjet and VideaHealth price per location or usage and Pearl per user per month, with no figures given (overjet.com/blog/cost-of-dental-ai-overjet-vs-pearl-vs-videahealth, 22 Apr 2025, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]). The dental-office plan below at about $5.65 a month is 1.9% of the $300 average [D].

Web upload and a plug-in for the film-capture software dental offices and radiology clinics already use; sales through dental associations, equipment and film-sensor suppliers; a free trial to individual offices.

Free first 10 scans [A]; every finding is labelled as a suggestion for clinician confirmation; the 3% sample audited by a specialist is reported back to the clinic as an accuracy log [A]; one customer-success person per 60 accounts [A]. Monthly plan billed in toman, indexed to the exchange rate.

Monthly by number of scans: Dental office 1,500,000 toman for 100 scans (about $5.65), Radiology clinic 15,000,000 for 1,500 scans (about $56.54), Chain or hospital 60,000,000 for 8,000 scans (about $226.16) [A, no Iranian competitor price was found]. Mix 80% / 17% / 3% [A] gives ARPU 5,550,000 toman a month (about $20.92) [D].

A licensed or self-trained image model for panoramic and chest films, with a labelled Iranian sample for testing (open medical-image models often carry non-commercial or research licences; I confirmed none); a report-writing vision-language or 8B-class text model; specialist time for the 3% audit; a domestic GPU node (RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, Sindad plan 150M toman a month [S]); 2 engineers, 1 customer-success hire and a 120M toman gross a month specialist and annotation budget [A].

Collecting and labelling films with consent; measuring sensitivity and false alarms per finding at each clinic; specialist audit of a sample; integration with capture software; keeping images and notes secure.

Domestic GPU/cloud host; payment gateway (Zarinpal and similar, worst-case 1% fee [S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%]); a radiologist and a dental specialist as clinical advisers; equipment and software suppliers; dental and radiology associations as channels.

Fixed: team 307.5M toman a month (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-success at 30M + 120M specialist and annotation budget, gross [A] × 1.23 [S]), GPU node 150M, other infrastructure 15M, accounting 8M, marketing 30M = 510.5M toman a month (about $1,924) [D]; one-time setup 600M [A] (labelled test and training films, clinical validation and legal review). Variable: gateway 1% of revenue, 2,500 toman per scan for the 3% specialist audit [A], an extra customer-success hire per 60 accounts [A], an extra GPU node when load passes one node's capacity.
[D] (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-success at 30M + 120M specialist and annotation budget, gross, salaries [A]) × 1.23 employer insurance [S]
[S] Sindad GPU inference plan, listed 14 Sep 2026
[A] about 0.5 s for a detection and segmentation model plus about 1.5 s for the report text from a vision-language or text model, on one RTX 6000 Ada; a non-text proxy, not measured
[A] films arrive in office hours and in bursts
[A] 3% of scans audited by a radiologist or dental specialist, 10 minutes each at a loaded 500,000 toman an hour (83,333 per audit)
[D] 80% use [A] of the 100 / 1,500 / 8,000 quotas, weighted by plan mix
Dental office 83.6%, Radiology clinic 75.9%, Chain or hospital 68.2%

cost_model.x: One node covers about 827 accounts at this usage [D: 388,800 ÷ (460 + 10 free-trial scans)], so the base case needs one node at month 24 and the optimistic case two [D]. The specialist audit is 87% of variable cost per scan [D: 2,500 ÷ 2,886] and the node is 29% of fixed cost [D: 150 ÷ 510.5], so the audit rate matters more than the GPU speed. Customer-success staffing at one hire per 60 accounts costs 615,000 toman a month per account [D: 36.9M ÷ 60], 11% of revenue per account. The cost of building or licensing the image model is only the 600M setup guess; clinician review of every flagged film is not priced.

revenue.x: Break-even is about 118 paying accounts on the fixed-cost formula [D: 510.5M ÷ (5,550,000 × 0.99 − 460 × 2,500) = 117.5], and stepping through account counts with the node and hires each needs gives 135 accounts [D]. Accounts ramp linearly from month 4 to the month-12 figure, then to the month-24 figure; the 600M setup falls in month 1.

Account counts are [A]. At month 24 the base case is about 450 accounts and 207,000 scans a month [D: 450 × 460]; the optimistic case is about 960 dental offices, 4.5% of the rough 21,242 pool [D], plus about 204 radiology clinics and 36 chains, for which I found no population. Cumulative cash at month 24 is −6,888M toman in the conservative case (payback beyond month 24, so the peak cash need of 6,983M came earlier), +3,536M in the base case and +27,970M in the optimistic case [D].

sensitivities.x: No single stress removes break-even in the base case, and the GPU price barely matters because the node is a small part of cost; the month-24 profit is most exposed to price and to the account count. Churn is not in the cash rows (the customer path is fixed). At 4% monthly churn [A, clinics keep a tool that is built into the capture step] lifetime value per account is about 108.6M toman [D: (5,550,000 × 0.99 − 460 × 2,500) ÷ 0.04], and holding 450 accounts needs about 18 new accounts a month [D: 450 × 0.04]. Marketing cost per account was not modelled separately; measure it in a pilot.

risks.x: Accuracy: I found no public sensitivity or false-alarm figure for an image model on Iranian clinics' films; missed lesions or false alarms would turn the tool into extra work, and the 3% audit rate would have to rise (at 10% the audit cost per scan is about 8,333 toman [D: 83,333 × 10%], which would cut the dental-office plan's gross margin to about 41% [D] and make the chain plan, at 7,500 toman a scan, loss-making).

Image-model licence: open medical-image models are often research or non-commercial; none was confirmed, so the service may require training a model on licensed data, which the 600M setup does not cover.

Device rules: diagnostic software may need registration as a medical device with the health ministry; I found no Iranian rule, so the product is described as a second reader and clinical liability stays with the clinician [A].
Patient data: films are health data; clinics are likely to require domestic hosting and consent [A]; I found no specific rule.
Adoption: dentists who read films quickly may see little value, and capture software from equipment vendors may not accept add-ons.
Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 [D]).

unverified.x: Sensitivity and false-alarm rates of any image model on panoramic or chest films from Iranian clinics, and the licence of any open model that reaches them.
Whether Iranian rules classify diagnostic image software as a regulated medical device, and what approval it needs.
The number of radiology clinics, how many films a dental office takes a month, and the private-practice share of dentists (60% is an assumption).
Any Iranian price for image-reading or dental-AI software.
Real GPU time per film (2.0 seconds is an assumption).
Zarinpal fee and VAT, as in #1.
Check run: all [D] figures above were recomputed by running the model in code on 26 Oct 2026.

verdict_blocks.x: Verdict: marginal. The service is cheap to run, about 319 toman (about $0.0012) per daily order proposal with gross margin around 98% [D], so the result depends almost entirely on how many pharmacies pay and on a small team's fixed cost. Revenue per account is about 1.50M toman a month ($5.67) against 407.1M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 274 paying accounts on paper and 373 with the node and hires counted [D]. The base case (150 accounts at month 12, 600 at month 24) breaks even in month 18, with a peak cash need of 4,394M toman (about $16,561) and +227M a month at month 24, but cumulative cash is still −3,643M then, so it has not paid back; the conservative case (60 / 200) never breaks even in 24 months, with a peak cash need of 7,293M and −183M at month 24; the optimistic case (300 / 1,200) breaks even in month 13 with +825M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 22, while cutting prices 30% or halving customers removes break-even within 24 months. Account counts are heavy because chains count as one account but several branches, and the 8,500-pharmacy pool is an undated figure [S]. The tool forecasts demand and expiry from the pharmacy's own sales; it cannot forecast supply shortages, and I could not verify how pharmacy software, wholesaler lists or the national track-and-trace system would give it data. Substitution hints are suggestions for the pharmacist only. Customer counts are hypotheses [A]. Tags: [S] sourced, [D] derived and recomputed by code, [A] assumption.

r: (a) Independent community pharmacies — core. (b) Pharmacy chains and groups of branches. (c) Hospital pharmacies and wholesalers' retail arms. Pool: about 8,500 pharmacies in Iran (Chemanager, chemanager-online.com/en/node/418762, read 26 Oct 2026; the page gives no year and its market figure is for 2015, so the count is probably several years old [S]). At month 24 the base case has 600 accounts: about 360 single pharmacies, 192 with alerts and 48 chains of 10 branches, covering about 1,032 pharmacies, 12.1% of the pool [D]; the optimistic case covers about 2,064, 24.3% [D], which is a very high share; the conservative case about 344, 4.0% [D].

Each morning the tool turns the pharmacy's sales and stock export into a proposed order (what to reorder, how much), flags items that will expire before they sell, and, when a product is short at the wholesaler, suggests same-ingredient alternatives matched through Iranian brand names. The labour replaced is the daily stock and expiry check: 20 minutes per order [A], about 47,674 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance [D]); the plans charge 26,667–40,000 toman per proposal, 56–84% of that [D]. Context [S]: Stimson reports that as many as 300 drug types were in short supply and about 100 unavailable (citing IRNA), most prices rose 15% to over 150%, about $35 million of pharmacy cheques to drug companies bounced and 3 in 10 patients abandon a purchase at checkout (stimson.org/2025/irans-dire-and-growing-drug-shortage, 2025, read 26 Oct 2026); Iran International reported on 13 Dec 2025 that suppliers warned of worsening shortages (iranintl.com/en/202512136473, lead only). Foreign anchors: inventory software with expiry tracking such as Vencru lists at $0, $6, $30 and $50 a month, and general inventory tools such as Zoho Inventory at $39–$299 a month [S, vencru.com/blog/7-best-inventory-management-software-for-pharmacy, published 24 May 2024, modified 20 May 2025, read 26 Oct 2026; currency not stated, presumed USD]; the single-pharmacy plan below at about $3.02 a month is 50% of the $6 plan [D]. A vendor blog says one chain cut excess inventory by 50% across 332 locations with AI replenishment, with no year or baseline (leafio.ai/blog/pharmacy-inventory-management, updated 29 Apr 2026 [S], vendor claim).

Web app and a data-export connector for the pharmacy software in use; sales through pharmacist associations, wholesaler sales representatives and pharmacy-software vendors; a free first month to individual pharmacies.

revenue.x: Break-even is about 274 paying accounts on the fixed-cost formula [D: 407.1M ÷ (1,504,000 × 0.99 − 43.9 × 30) = 273.7], and stepping through account counts with the node and hires each needs gives 373 accounts [D]. At month 24 the base case covers about 1,032 pharmacies, 12.1% of the 8,500 pool [D, above]; the optimistic case about 2,064 (24.3%) and the conservative case about 344 (4.0%) [D]. Shortage forecasting: shortages come from supply, price and import decisions, not from a pharmacy's sales; the tool can only react to a wholesaler's out-of-stock list, which I did not find in machine-readable form.

Revenue per account is about 2.31M toman a month ($8.71) against 431.7M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 191 paying accounts on paper and 224 with the node and hires counted [D]. The base case (100 accounts at month 12, 400 at month 24) breaks even in month 17, with a peak cash need of 4,488M toman (about $16,919) and +290M a month at month 24, but cumulative cash is still −3,314M then; the conservative case (40 / 150) never breaks even in 24 months, with a peak cash need of 7,387M and −129M at month 24; the optimistic case (250 / 1,000) breaks even in month 12 with +1,240M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 21 and cutting prices 30% to month 23; halving customers removes it. The decisive gap is the interaction knowledge itself: the commercial references I found are priced and licensed abroad, and I did not find an open interaction dataset with a licence that allows resale, nor a mapping of Iranian brand names to ingredients. A wrong or missed interaction is a patient-safety matter, so the output must stay advisory. Customer counts are hypotheses [A]. Tags: [S] sourced, [D] derived and recomputed by code, [A] assumption.

Pool: about 8,500 pharmacies in Iran (Chemanager, chemanager-online.com/en/node/418762, read 26 Oct 2026; undated, market figure for 2015 [S]). A 2025 study projects 40,349 pharmacists in 2032 against demand of 26,888–28,538, a surplus of about 11,800–13,500 (Medical Journal of the Islamic Republic of Iran, mjiri.iums.ac.ir/article-1-9610-en.html, Jan 2025, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]); it gives no current count. The decisive gaps are demand and safety: I found no evidence that Iranian labs would pay to explain results, and the one 2026 industry article I opened says AI models are not benchmarked for lab results, with no strong clinical evidence on their reliability, and that software interpreting a diagnosis is generally treated as a medical device abroad. The service is therefore sold to labs as a plain-language explanation with a referral line, never as a diagnosis. Customer counts are hypotheses [A]. Tags: [S] sourced, [D] derived and recomputed by code, [A] assumption.

r: (a) Independent medical laboratories that deliver results by SMS, web or paper — core. (b) Mid-size labs and hospital laboratories. (c) Lab networks and online result portals. Not targeted: patients directly (high acquisition cost, one-off use). Pool: a study of the Iranian laboratory network reports more than 7,300 laboratories active in the national monitoring system, about 4,000 of them in the treatment sector (mainly public and private medical laboratories) and more than 3,200 in the health sector, with no public-private split and no year stated beyond a 2021 context (Journal of Health, doh.tbzmed.ac.ir/PDF/doh-13-11.pdf, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]). Using 4,000 as the pool [A, treatment-sector labs], the base case at month 24 (150 labs) is 3.75% of it [D].

Next to each result, the patient gets a plain Persian explanation: what each test measures, whether the value is inside the lab's printed reference range, which results deserve a doctor's visit soon, and common non-diagnostic notes, with a fixed disclaimer. The labour replaced is staff time answering patients' questions: 3 minutes per report [A], about 7,151 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance [D]); the plans charge 2,000–3,000 toman per report, 28–42% of that [D]. Foreign anchors: consumer lab-explanation apps are freemium or a few dollars per report or month, with subscriptions of about $4–$8 a month, wellness bundles from $199 a test or about $500 a year, and lab-facing tools priced per report or per analyte, sometimes in cents (Dark Daily, darkdaily.com, 20 Apr 2026, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]); one consumer app, MedInsight, sells $5.99 a week, $11.99 a month, $29.99 for 6 months and $59.99 a year (Apple App Store listing, apps.apple.com/np/app/medinsight-lab-results-ai/id6744040532, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]). The per-report price here is about $0.0075–$0.0113 [D].
Direct sales to lab owners; integration with the lab information system or the SMS result link; sales through laboratory associations; a pilot of 500 free reports per lab.

Free first 20 reports [A]; lab-branded pages; the lab sets which results trigger a call-back; physician review of the 2% of reports with critical values [A]; one customer-success person per 40 labs [A] (integration support). Monthly plan billed in toman, indexed to the exchange rate.

Monthly by number of reports: Small lab 6,000,000 toman for 2,000 reports (about $22.62), Mid-size lab 20,000,000 for 8,000 reports (about $75.39), Lab network 100,000,000 for 50,000 reports (about $376.93) [A, no Iranian competitor price was found]. Mix 70% / 27% / 3% [A] gives ARPU 12,600,000 toman a month (about $47.49) [D].

Domestic GPU/cloud host; payment gateway (Zarinpal and similar, worst-case 1% fee [S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%]); lab information-system vendors; a pathologist or physician adviser; laboratory associations.

cost_model.x: One node covers about 182 accounts at this usage [D: 740,571 ÷ (4,048 + 20 free-trial reports)], so the base case needs one node at month 24 and the optimistic case three [D]. The physician review is 81% of variable cost per report [D: 850 ÷ 1,052], so the share of reports flagged matters more than GPU speed. Customer-success staffing at one hire per 40 labs costs 922,500 toman a month per account [D: 36.9M ÷ 40], 7% of revenue per account. Liability insurance and the cost of a wrong explanation are not priced.

revenue.x: Break-even is about 48 paying labs on the fixed-cost formula [D: 431.7M ÷ (12,600,000 × 0.99 − 4,048 × 850) = 47.8], and stepping through account counts with the node and hires each needs gives 52 labs [D]. Accounts ramp linearly from month 4 to the month-12 figure, then to the month-24 figure; the 200M setup falls in month 1.

Lab counts are [A]. At month 24 the base case is about 150 labs explaining 607,200 reports a month [D: 150 × 4,048], 3.75% of the 4,000 treatment-sector labs [D]; the optimistic case is 400 labs, 10% [D], and the conservative case 60 labs, 1.5% [D]. Cumulative cash at month 24 is −5,427M toman in the conservative case (payback beyond month 24, so the peak cash need of 5,545M came earlier), +1,528M in the base case and +18,145M in the optimistic case [D].

sensitivities.x: No single stress removes break-even in the base case, but a price cut or fewer labs cuts month-24 profit by about 70%. Churn is not in the cash rows (the customer path is fixed). At 3% monthly churn [A, labs keep a feature that patients use] lifetime value per account is about 301.1M toman [D: (12,600,000 × 0.99 − 4,048 × 850) ÷ 0.03], and holding 150 labs needs about 5 new labs a month [D: 150 × 0.03 = 4.5]. risks.x: Clinical safety: a model that misreads a unit or a range could reassure a patient with a dangerous result; the explanation quotes the lab's printed ranges and critical values route to a physician, and the 2% review rate [A] may be too low until accuracy is measured.
Accuracy evidence: the 2026 industry article says AI models are not benchmarked for lab results and clinical evidence of reliability is lacking [S, Dark Daily, 20 Apr 2026].
Regulation and liability: abroad, software that interprets a diagnosis is generally a medical device [S, same article]; I found no Iranian rule, and labs may refuse the liability.
Demand: labs deliver results quickly and patients can ask a free chatbot; I found no evidence that labs would pay [A].
Integration: labs use varied information systems, and reports arrive as PDF or image, so parsing cost may exceed the 200M setup.
Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 [D]).

The accuracy of any model on Iranian lab-report layouts, units and Persian text.
Whether Iranian rules treat result-explanation software as a medical device, and who is liable.
How many reports a typical Iranian laboratory issues a month (the 2,000 / 8,000 / 50,000 quotas are assumptions).
Real GPU and OCR time per report (1.4 seconds is an assumption).
Zarinpal fee and VAT, as in #1.

verdict_blocks.x: Verdict: viable on the numbers, but the demand evidence is thin: I found no count of Iranian clinics and no data on claim volumes. A claim costs about 3,353 toman (about $0.0126) to check, including GPU time on a 15-page file and a 2% specialist re-check, and gross margin is 54–77% by plan [D]; the plans charge 6,000–12,000 toman per claim against about 14,302 toman of insurance-liaison staff time at the minimum wage [D]. Revenue per account is about 22.3M toman a month ($84.13) against 431.7M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 25 paying accounts on paper and 25 with the node and hires counted [D]. The base case (60 accounts at month 12, 250 at month 24) breaks even in month 7, with a peak cash need of 1,836M toman (about $6,920) and +2,584M a month at month 24 (cumulative cash +17,754M); the conservative case (25 / 100) breaks even in month 12 with a peak cash need of 2,944M and +752M at month 24; the optimistic case (150 / 600) breaks even in month 6 with +6,598M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 11, cutting prices 30% to month 13 and halving customers to month 11. These results rest on three assumptions I could not source: that a hospital files about 6,000 claims a month, that a file takes 10 seconds of GPU time, and that hospitals will let a vendor read patient files. The real problem is documented: a meta-analysis found about 5% of claimed amounts denied in Iranian hospitals and documentation faults the most common cause, which is what a pre-check targets, but I found no evidence on how much of it software can prevent. Account counts are hypotheses [A]. Tags: [S] sourced, [D] derived and recomputed by code, [A] assumption.

r: (a) Private clinics and day-surgery centres that bill insurers — core by count. (b) Hospitals, public and private, which employ insurance-liaison staff — core by revenue. (c) Hospital groups. Not targeted: insurers' own review departments (a possible second product). Pool: a count from 2003 lists 730 hospital and clinic establishments with 110,797 beds, 488 of them public and 120 private (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare\_in\_Iran, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]; 23 years old, so it is a floor for hospitals only). The same page says more than 90% of the population has health insurance, with no year, and names the Social Security Organization, the Medical Service Insurance Organization, the Imam Khomeini Relief Foundation and the military personnel insurer among the insurers [S]. At month 24 the base case has about 150 clinics, 92 hospitals and 8 hospital groups [D]; the 92 hospitals are 12.6% of the 730 [D]. I found no count of clinics.

Before a file goes to the insurer, the tool reads the discharge summary, orders, signatures, stamps and tariff lines and lists the faults that usually cause deductions (missing signature or stamp, unsupported imaging or drugs, quantities outside the tariff), so staff fix them first. The labour replaced is the manual check: 6 minutes per claim [A], about 14,302 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance [D]); the plans charge 6,000–12,000 toman per claim, 42–84% of that [D]. The problem is documented: a systematic review and meta-analysis of Iranian hospital studies found about 5% of claimed amounts denied (95% interval 2.88–7.12) and 45.2% of inpatient records with some denial (interval 17.6–72.8, very high heterogeneity), with documentation problems the most common cause at 17.96% (Journal of Health Reports and Technology, brieflands.com/articles/jhrt-121200.html, published 19 Apr 2022, studies from about 2008 to 2021, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]; the paper's own counts of 16 and 14 included studies are inconsistent). Foreign anchors: clearinghouses charge $0.25–$1.00 per claim and eligibility checks $0.15–$0.35, flat subscriptions run $30–$150 per provider a month (enter.health, 22 Apr 2026, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]); the per-claim price here is about $0.023–$0.045 [D], 2–18% of the foreign per-claim range, and the clinic plan at $22.62 a month is 75% of the $30 flat fee [D].
Direct sales to hospital insurance and finance managers; integration with the hospital information system; sales through hospital-software vendors; a pilot on one month's rejected files.

Free first 20 claims [A]; a monthly report of faults found against deductions received; the 2% re-check by a specialist feeds an accuracy log [A]; one customer-success person per 30 accounts [A] because each integration is manual. Monthly plan billed in toman, indexed to the exchange rate.

Monthly by number of claims: Clinic 6,000,000 toman for 500 claims (about $22.62), Hospital 36,000,000 for 6,000 claims (about $135.70), Hospital group 180,000,000 for 30,000 claims (about $678.49) [A, no Iranian competitor price was found]. Mix 60% / 37% / 3% [A] gives ARPU 22,320,000 toman a month (about $84.13) [D].

A rule base of insurer tariffs and documentation requirements that is kept current; a document reader for scanned dossiers (a non-text proxy); an 8B-class instruction model that applies the rules and cites the page; a domestic GPU node (RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, Sindad plan 150M toman a month [S]); 2 engineers, 1 customer-success hire and a 60M gross a month insurance-claims specialist [A].
Writing and updating rules per insurer and tariff year; reading dossiers; measuring faults found against later deductions; integrating with hospital systems; protecting patient files.

Domestic GPU/cloud host; payment gateway (Zarinpal and similar, worst-case 1% fee [S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%]); hospital-software vendors; an experienced hospital insurance-liaison adviser; possibly the insurers.

Fixed: team 233.7M toman a month (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-success at 30M + 60M claims specialist, gross [A] × 1.23 [S]), GPU node 150M, other infrastructure 10M, accounting 8M, marketing 30M = 431.7M toman a month (about $1,627) [D]; one-time setup 350M [A] (rule base, dossier reader and test files). Variable: gateway 1% of revenue, 1,700 toman per claim for the 2% specialist re-check [A], an extra customer-success hire per 30 accounts [A], an extra GPU node when load passes one node's capacity.

[S] Sindad GPU inference plan, listed 14 Sep 2026

[A] a 15-page file: reading about 0.5 s a page = 7.5 s (a non-text proxy, not measured) plus rule-checking text 2.2 s [D: (4,000 tokens in + 600 out [A]) ÷ (2,658.57 tokens a second [S, A6000 vLLM benchmark, Llama-3.1-8B] × 0.8 [A])], rounded up

cost_model.x: One node covers only about 33 accounts at this usage [D: 90,720 ÷ (2,736 + 20 free-trial claims)], so GPU nodes scale with customers: the base case needs 8 nodes at month 24 and the optimistic case 19 [D]; nodes are 40% of base-case cost at month 24 [D: 1,200M of 2,996M]. The reading time per page is the most uncertain input. Customer-success staffing at one hire per 30 accounts costs 1,230,000 toman a month per account [D: 36.9M ÷ 30], 5.5% of revenue per account. Security work for patient files and any legal cost of insurer disputes are not priced.

revenue.x: Break-even is about 25 paying accounts on the fixed-cost formula [D: 431.7M ÷ (22,320,000 × 0.99 − 2,736 × 1,700) = 24.7], and stepping through account counts with the node and hires each needs gives 25 accounts [D]. Accounts ramp linearly from month 4 to the month-12 figure, then to the month-24 figure; the 350M setup falls in month 1.

Account counts are [A]. At month 24 the base case is about 250 accounts checking 684,000 claims a month [D: 250 × 2,736]; the optimistic case is about 600 accounts, of which about 222 hospitals [D: 600 × 37%], 30% of the 730 hospital establishments counted in 2003 [D], which is a high share. Cumulative cash at month 24 is +2,143M toman in the conservative case, +17,754M in the base case and +55,243M in the optimistic case [D]; the peak cash need came earlier in each.

sensitivities.x: Every stress keeps break-even within 13 months, but all of them lean on one hospital buying decision and on a claim volume of 6,000 a month that I could not check, and the GPU stress is the nearest proxy for a slower page-reading speed than assumed. Churn is not in the cash rows (the customer path is fixed). At 3% monthly churn [A, a pre-check built into the billing routine is sticky] lifetime value per account is about 581.5M toman [D: (22,320,000 × 0.99 − 2,736 × 1,700) ÷ 0.03], and holding 250 accounts needs about 8 new accounts a month [D: 250 × 0.03 = 7.5]. Marketing cost per account was not modelled separately; measure it in a pilot.

risks.x: Value proof: a hospital pays only if it recovers more than the plan costs; with 20% fewer denials [A] a 36M toman plan for 4,800 used claims needs an average claim above about 750,000 toman to pay back at the 5% denial rate [D: 36M ÷ (4,800 × 5% × 20%)]; I found no average claim value.
Patient files: dossiers hold full clinical records; hospitals may refuse an outside vendor or demand on-site installation, which would change the cost model.
Rule changes: insurer tariffs and requirements change often, and I found no machine-readable source; the rule base is a permanent cost.
Insurers: insurers could build the same check or reject files from vendors, and I did not verify their rules on pre-submission tools.
Evidence: the 5% and 45% figures come from a heterogeneous review (I² = 99.6%) of studies up to 2021 [S].
Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 [D]).

unverified.x: The number of Iranian clinics and the current number of hospitals (730 is from 2003).
Claim volumes per clinic or hospital, average claim value, and what share of denials software can prevent.
Any Iranian price for claim checking or hospital insurance software.
Rules on sending patient files to an outside processor.
Real GPU time per 15-page file (10 seconds is an assumption with a non-text proxy).
Zarinpal fee and VAT, as in #1.
Check run: all [D] figures above were recomputed by running the model in code on 26 Oct 2026.

verdict_blocks.x: Verdict: viable on the numbers, but whether Iranians will pay for it is unproven, and the marketing budget I assumed is probably too low. An interaction (a meal-photo analysis or a coach message) costs about 358 toman (about $0.00135) to serve, and gross margin is 79–87% by plan [D]; the plans charge 2,333–8,333 toman per interaction, against about 11,919 toman of dietitian time at the minimum wage for a 5-minute estimate [D]. Revenue per subscriber is about 640,000 toman a month ($2.41) against 732.45M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 1,291 paying subscribers on one GPU node [D]. The base case (3,000 subscribers at month 12, 12,000 at month 24) breaks even in month 7, with a peak cash need of 2,289M toman (about $8,629) and +5,595M a month at month 24; the conservative case (1,000 / 4,000) breaks even in month 14 with a peak cash need of 5,004M and +1,477M at month 24; the optimistic case (8,000 / 30,000) breaks even in month 5 with +14,786M. The 300M a month marketing budget implies only about 175,000 toman ($0.66) per new paying subscriber at month 24 [D], which I could not support from any source: with marketing at four times that level, base break-even moves to month 12 with a peak cash need of 7,567M and +4,695M at month 24, and the conservative case breaks even in month 20 with a peak cash need of 16,684M [D]. Open risks: I found no Iranian price for a diet app or a dietitian visit, the only Iranian food-composition table I found is listed as restricted access, and I could not verify that a 7B vision model recognises Iranian dishes or portions well enough to give calorie estimates. Subscriber counts are hypotheses [A]. Tags: [S] sourced, [D] derived and recomputed by code, [A] assumption.

r: (a) Adults who want to lose weight or manage a condition and eat Iranian home cooking, the core by count. (b) People with diabetes, hypertension or high cholesterol who want meal guidance between doctor visits, a sub-segment of (a). (c) Gym members and fitness-minded users who want a combined food and training plan. Not targeted: patients who need a clinical diet prescribed by a hospital dietitian. Pool: Iran had 92.6M people and 73.8M internet users (79.6%) in October 2025 (DataReportal Digital 2026, datareportal.com/reports/digital-2026-iran, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]); 76.8% of the population was aged 15 or over (0–14 years 23.3%, 2024 estimate; Wikipedia Demographics of Iran, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]), about 71.1M [D]; 63.0% of Iranian adults had overweight or obesity in the STEPs 2021 survey (Frontiers in Endocrinology, 2022, frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2022.1043894/full, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]; the abstract and body text disagree on the sex split, 66% / 53% against 61.5% / 54.5%). That gives about 44.8M adults with overweight or obesity, and about 35.7M of them online if internet use is independent of weight [D; 15+ population used where the survey covers adults, so approximate]. The base case has 12,000 paying subscribers at month 24, 0.034% of that pool [D]. Karafs, an Iranian calorie-counter app founded in 2014, is listed with over 2 million registered users, but the Dealroom text is labelled as AI-generated (app.dealroom.co/companies/karafs, read 26 Oct 2026 [S, unverified]), so 12,000 subscribers would be 0.6% of that number [D].

The user photographs a meal or types it in Persian (for example ghormeh sabzi with rice, or a kebab plate), and the coach estimates energy and macros, compares them with the user's daily target, and suggests the next meal and a short home or gym workout from local foods and habits. The labour replaced is a dietitian estimating one meal and replying: 5 minutes [A], about 11,919 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance [D]); the plans charge 2,333–8,333 toman per interaction, 20–70% of that [D]. That compares a minimum-wage person, not a real dietitian fee, which I could not find. Foreign anchor: MyFitnessPal Premium costs $19.99 a month or $79.99 a year, and Premium+ $24.99 or $99.99 (FitBudd, published 12 Jan 2026, updated 21 Sep 2026, fitbudd.com/post/myfitnesspal-app-cost, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]); the annual Premium price is about $6.67 a month, about 1.77M toman [D], so the Basic plan at 300,000 toman is 17% of it, Plus 40%, and the blended 640,000 toman 36% [D]. The Premium plan at 2,500,000 toman is 141% of it because it includes a monthly dietitian review.

Cafe Bazaar and Myket listings (their commissions were not verified); Instagram and Telegram content on Iranian dishes with calories; partnerships with gyms and dietitian clinics; referral codes; a free tier of 5 interactions.

Daily coach messages and weekly progress summaries; a monthly 10-minute dietitian review for Premium [A]; one customer-support person per 2,000 subscribers [A]; cancellation at any time because most competitors are freemium. Monthly plan billed in toman, indexed to the exchange rate.

Monthly subscription by interaction quota: Basic 300,000 toman for 90 interactions (about $1.13), Plus 700,000 for 300 (about $2.64), Premium 2,500,000 for 300 plus a monthly dietitian review (about $9.42) [A, no Iranian competitor price was found]. Mix 60% / 30% / 10% [A] gives ARPU 640,000 toman a month (about $2.41) [D].

A Persian food and portion database (a licensed or self-built table: the Iranian Food Composition Table 2017 from the National Nutrition and Food Technology Research Institute is held in EuroFIR FoodEXplorer and listed as restricted access, with no licence stated, FAO INFOODS page, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]); a 7B-class vision-language model for meal photos (a non-text proxy); a domestic GPU node (RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, Sindad plan 150M toman a month [S]); 2 engineers, 1 customer-support hire and 2 dietitians at 45M gross each a month [A].

Building and checking Persian dish recipes and portions; testing photo estimates against weighed meals; writing safety rules (no crash diets, referral advice for medical conditions); running the monthly dietitian reviews; content and user acquisition.

Domestic GPU/cloud host; app stores (Cafe Bazaar, Myket); payment gateway (Zarinpal and similar, worst-case 1% fee [S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%]); gyms and dietitians; the food-composition institute if a licence can be agreed.

Fixed: team 264.45M toman a month (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-support at 25M + 2 dietitians at 45M, gross [A] × 1.23 [S]), GPU node 150M, other infrastructure 10M, accounting 8M, marketing 300M = 732.45M toman a month (about $2,761) [D]; one-time setup 250M [A] (food database build and weighed-meal tests). Variable: payment and app-store fees 10% of revenue [A], 68.4 toman per interaction for the Premium dietitian review [A], an extra support hire per 2,000 subscribers [A], an extra GPU node when load passes one node's capacity.
[D] (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-support at 25M + 2 dietitians at 45M, gross, salaries [A]) × 1.23 employer insurance [S]
[S] Sindad GPU inference plan, listed 14 Sep 2026

[A] a meal photo of about 900 tokens in and 300 out on a 7B vision-language model; Qwen2.5-VL-7B on an L40S gave 832 tokens a second at 32 concurrent requests with a 512 px image (Clarifai, 26 Jun 2025 [S]), which appears to count generated tokens (346 requests a minute × 150 out) [A reading]; × 0.67 for an RTX 6000 Ada [A] = 557 tokens a second, so 300 tokens take 0.54 s [D]; 1.5 s allows for the image prefill and uneven batching; text-only coach messages are faster; not measured

[A] each Premium subscriber (10% of the mix) gets a 10-minute dietitian review a month at a loaded 500,000 toman an hour (83,333), which is 8,333 per average subscriber [D], spread over 121.8 interactions
[D] 70% use [A] of the 90 / 300 / 300 quotas, weighted by plan mix (average quota 174)
[D] after GPU, dietitian review and the 10% payment and store fee [A]

cost_model.x: One node covers about 4,088 subscribers at this usage [D: 518,400 ÷ (121.8 + 5 free-trial interactions)], so the base case needs 3 nodes at month 24 and the optimistic case 8; nodes are 22% of base-case cost at month 24 [D: 450M of 2,085M]. Support at one hire per 2,000 subscribers costs 15,375 toman a month per subscriber [D: 30.75M ÷ 2,000], 2.4% of revenue per subscriber. The vision speed and the 10% store fee are the least certain inputs. Any cost of licensing food data, of insuring against bad advice, or of legal review is not priced beyond the 250M setup.

revenue.x: Break-even is about 1,291 paying subscribers on the fixed-cost formula [D: 732.45M ÷ (640,000 × 0.90 − 121.8 × 68.4) = 1,290.3], and stepping through subscriber counts with the node and support hires each needs also gives 1,291 on one node [D]. Subscribers ramp linearly from month 4 to the month-12 figure, then to the month-24 figure; the 250M setup falls in month 1.

Subscriber counts are [A]. At month 24 the base case is about 12,000 subscribers sending 1.46M interactions a month [D: 12,000 × 121.8]; the optimistic 30,000 is 0.084% of the 35.7M online adults with overweight or obesity [D]. Cumulative cash at month 24 is +3,804M toman in the conservative case, +41,586M in the base case and +129,223M in the optimistic case [D]; the peak cash need came earlier in each.

r: Marketing four times higher (1,200M a month)

sensitivities.x: Every stress keeps break-even within 12 months, but all of them lean on the same untested fact, that tens of thousands of Iranians will pay a subscription for a diet coach when free apps and free chatbots exist. The last row is an extra stress I added because the base marketing budget implies a very low acquisition cost. Churn is not in the cash rows (the customer path is fixed). At 8% monthly churn [A, consumer diet apps lose users quickly] lifetime value per subscriber is about 7.10M toman [D: (640,000 × 0.90 − 121.8 × 68.4) ÷ 0.08]. Holding 12,000 subscribers needs about 960 replacements a month [D: 12,000 × 0.08], plus 750 net additions a month in the second year [D], so about 1,710 new subscribers a month; 300M of marketing then buys each one for about 175,000 toman [D], which I could not check against any source.

risks.x: Willingness to pay: I found no Iranian diet-app price, and Karafs is described as freemium with paid plans for advanced features (Dealroom text, AI-labelled [S, unverified]); if most users stay on a free tier the subscriber counts here do not hold.

Estimate accuracy and harm: calorie and portion estimates from a photo are uncertain, and wrong advice to a person with diabetes or hypertension could cause harm; the Premium dietitian review and referral rules cost money and I could not verify what Iranian rules allow an automated service to say.

Food data: the only Iranian food-composition table I found is listed as restricted access with no stated licence [S]; if it cannot be licensed, building a table of Iranian dishes and portions costs more than the 250M assumed.

Model capability: a 7B vision model may confuse similar dishes and misjudge rice and oil quantities, and its Persian chat quality was not tested; a larger model would raise GPU cost, and the GPU-doubling row is the nearest proxy.
Free substitutes: general chatbots and international apps can answer food questions at no charge to users who can reach them.
Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 [D]).

unverified.x: Any Iranian price for a diet-app subscription or a dietitian visit (the Doctoreto dietitian pages, Cafe Bazaar lists and the Karafs App Store page are blocked or not fetchable, and the Persian app-review articles were titles only).
Paying-user numbers or free-to-paid conversion for any Iranian diet app, and whether Karafs really has 2 million registered users.
Accuracy of a 7B vision model on Iranian dishes and portions, and real GPU time per interaction (1.5 seconds is an assumption).
Licence, size and access terms of the Iranian Food Composition Table.
Rules on automated diet advice and on handling users' health data.
Cafe Bazaar and Myket commissions, and the Zarinpal fee and VAT, as in #1.
The exact adult (18+) population; I used the 15+ share and an STEPs sex split that the source states inconsistently.
Check run: all [D] figures above were recomputed by running the model in code on 26 Oct 2026.

verdict_blocks.x: Verdict: marginal, and thin on demand evidence. A session note costs about 1,165 toman (about $0.0044) to produce, including 7.2 seconds of GPU time for a 3-minute voice dictation and a drafted note, and gross margin is 87–90% by plan [D]; the plans charge 8,000–10,000 toman per note against about 23,837 toman of a therapist's time at the minimum wage for a 10-minute note, which understates a therapist's real time [D]. Revenue per account is about 2.63M toman a month ($9.89) against 417.1M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 162 paying accounts on paper and 206 with the node and support hires counted [D]. The base case (90 accounts at month 12, 300 at month 24) breaks even in month 19, with a peak cash need of 4,369M toman (about $16,468) and +170M a month at month 24, but cumulative cash at month 24 is still −3,768M, so it has not paid back; the conservative case (30 / 100) does not break even, with a peak cash need of 7,548M and −197M at month 24; the optimistic case (200 / 600) breaks even in month 13 with +606M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 23, and cutting prices 30% or halving customers means no break-even within 24 months. The base case needs about 885 therapists, 18% of the roughly 5,000 licensed psychologists I found in one undated source [D]; I found no reliable count, no Iranian price for practice software, and no rule on storing session content. The product also depends on a Persian speech model that copes with therapists' vocabulary and on therapists being willing to dictate about clients to a cloud service, neither of which I could verify. Account counts are hypotheses [A]. Tags: [S] sourced, [D] derived and recomputed by code, [A] assumption.

r: (a) Solo psychologists and counsellors with a private practice, core by count. (b) Small practices of about 5 therapists. (c) Counselling centres of about 20 therapists, core by revenue per account. Not targeted: hospital psychiatry departments and the state counselling services. Pool: the Psychology and Counseling Organization of Iran, founded in 2003, issues the work licence (Pervaneh Eshteghal) to psychologists and counsellors (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychology\_and\_Counseling\_Organization\_of\_Iran, read 26 Oct 2026 [S]); one directory guide gives about 5,000 licensed practitioners with no date or source (therapyroute.com, Mental Health Licensing & Regulation in Iran 2025 guide, read 26 Oct 2026 [S, weak]), and a Tejarat News headline says 40,000 psychologists work without a licence (search result title only, undated, page blocked [S, headline]), so the true pool may be much larger or may be mostly unlicensed. An account averages 2.95 therapists in the assumed mix [D]. At month 24 the base case has about 210 solo accounts, 75 practices and 15 centres, 885 therapists in all, 18% of 5,000 [D]; the conservative case has 295 therapists (5.9%) and the optimistic case 1,770 (35%), which is high against the licensed count [D].

After each session the therapist dictates 3 minutes in Persian; the tool transcribes it, drafts a structured progress note from the therapist's template and the client's earlier notes, and flags missing items. It also books sessions, sends two reminder messages per session, and tracks cancellations. The labour replaced is writing the note: 10 minutes [A], about 23,837 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance [D]), which understates a therapist's time; the plans charge 8,000–10,000 toman per note, 34–42% of that [D]. Fee context from Persian press, search headlines only because the pages were blocked: a 45-minute counselling session from 750,000 to 2 million toman (Taadol newspaper, year unstated [S, headline]) and sessions sometimes reaching 5 million toman (Taadol, undated [S, headline]); at 750,000 toman the Solo plan's 1,000,000 toman a month is about 1.3 sessions' income [D]. Foreign anchors: SimplePractice $49 / $79 / $99 a month (Starter / Essential / Plus, verified 10 Jun 2026) plus an AI Note Taker add-on at $35 per clinician (checked 19 Oct 2026); TherapyNotes Solo $69 plus its AI add-on at $40; Mentalyc AI notes from $14.99 (Mentalyc blog, mentalyc.com/blog/simplepractice-vs-therapynotes, read 26 Oct 2026 [S, vendor blog]). The Solo price of $3.77 is 4.5% of SimplePractice Starter plus its AI add-on ($84) and 25% of Mentalyc's starting price [D].

Direct outreach to therapists through Instagram and Telegram; talks and training with the psychology and counselling organisation and university clinics; referral between therapists; a free first 10 notes.

Self-service onboarding with a template per therapy style; reminders and a monthly summary of sessions and cancellations; one customer-success person per 60 accounts [A] because templates need setup. Monthly plan billed in toman, indexed to the exchange rate.

Monthly subscription by number of notes: Solo 1,000,000 toman for 100 notes (about $3.77), Practice 4,500,000 for 500 (about $16.96), Centre 16,000,000 for 2,000 (about $60.31) [A, no Iranian competitor price was found]. Mix 70% / 25% / 5% [A] gives ARPU 2,625,000 toman a month (about $9.89) [D].

A Persian speech-to-text model that handles therapists' dictation (the open Persian leaderboard gives Whisper-large-v3 36–76% word error rate against 11–22% for navidved/gooya-v1.4, whose licence I could not confirm, leaderboard read 23 Oct 2026 [S]); an 8B-class instruction model for note drafting; note templates for the main therapy styles; a domestic GPU node (RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, Sindad plan 150M toman a month [S]); 2 engineers, 1 customer-success hire and a clinical psychologist adviser at 40M gross a month [A].
Building and testing templates with practising therapists; tuning speech recognition on therapy vocabulary; scheduling and reminder reliability; protecting stored notes; therapist outreach.

Domestic GPU/cloud host; SMS or messenger provider for reminders; payment gateway (Zarinpal and similar, worst-case 1% fee [S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%]); the psychology and counselling organisation or university clinics for access to therapists.

Fixed: team 209.1M toman a month (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-success at 30M + 40M adviser, gross [A] × 1.23 [S]), GPU node 150M, other infrastructure 10M, accounting 8M, marketing 40M = 417.1M toman a month (about $1,572) [D]; one-time setup 200M [A] (templates, speech tuning and tests). Variable: gateway 1% of revenue, 120 toman per note for storage and reminder messages [A], an extra customer-success hire per 60 accounts [A], an extra GPU node when load passes one node's capacity.

cost_model.x: One node covers about 584 accounts at this usage [D: 143,552 ÷ (236 + 10 free-trial notes)], so the base case needs one node through month 24 and the optimistic case two [D]; an idle node is 36% of base-case fixed cost at the start [D: 150M ÷ 417.1M], and a CPU-only deployment would change that but was not costed. Customer success at one hire per 60 accounts costs 615,000 toman a month per account [D: 36.9M ÷ 60], 23.4% of revenue per account, which is the largest cost that scales with customers. The speech speed and the 10-minute note time are the least certain inputs. Any legal or security cost of holding therapy records is not priced beyond the 200M setup.

revenue.x: Break-even is about 162 paying accounts on the fixed-cost formula [D: 417.1M ÷ (2,625,000 × 0.99 − 236 × 120) = 162.3], and stepping through account counts with the node and support hires each needs gives 206 accounts [D]. Accounts ramp linearly from month 4 to the month-12 figure, then to the month-24 figure; the 200M setup falls in month 1.

Account counts are [A]. At month 24 the base case is about 300 accounts writing 70,800 notes a month [D: 300 × 236]. Cumulative cash at month 24 is −7,548M toman in the conservative case, −3,768M in the base case and +2,181M in the optimistic case [D]; the peak cash need was reached at month 24 in the conservative case and earlier in the other two, and the base case has not repaid its cumulative cash need by month 24.

sensitivities.x: Two of the three stresses remove break-even within 24 months, and the base case itself turns profitable only in month 19, so the margin for error is thin. Churn is not in the cash rows (the customer path is fixed). At 4% monthly churn [A, practice software is sticky once notes are stored, but solo therapists may stop paying] lifetime value per account is about 64.3M toman [D: (2,625,000 × 0.99 − 236 × 120) ÷ 0.04], and holding 300 accounts needs about 12 new accounts a month [D: 300 × 0.04]. Marketing cost per account is about 1.36M toman at month 24 if 40M buys about 29.5 gross additions a month [D: 17.5 net + 12 replacements]; measure it in a pilot.

risks.x: Confidentiality: session content is among the most sensitive data a client shares; many therapists may refuse cloud dictation, or the licensing body may restrict it, which would shrink the pool far below the 5,000 figure.

Speech accuracy: Persian clinical and psychological vocabulary and mixed-language terms may push word error rates up; a 30 times speed assumption on a heavier model would raise GPU time, and the GPU-doubling row is the nearest proxy.

Willingness to pay: therapists already use paper, spreadsheets or free messengers for bookings, and I found no Iranian price for practice software; the Solo plan costs about 1.3 sessions' income at the lowest fee I saw in a headline, but the headline year is unknown.
Support load: at 23.4% of revenue per account, customer success is the largest scaling cost; if onboarding takes longer than assumed, break-even slips beyond month 19.
Platform risk: reminders depend on SMS or messenger access, whose retail prices and rules I could not verify.
Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 [D]).

unverified.x: The number of working psychologists and counsellors in Iran (5,000 is undated and unsourced; the 40,000 unlicensed figure is a headline only).
Any Iranian price for practice-management or note-taking software, and the fee a therapist currently charges per session (only headlines; the tariff pages were blocked).
Rules on recording or storing session content, and on holding client data outside the practice (the mental health law is described as still a draft in one directory guide, undated).
Accuracy of Persian speech recognition on therapy vocabulary, the licence of the open Persian ASR model, and real GPU time per note (7.2 seconds is an assumption).
Retail price of reminder messages (50 toman each is an assumption).
Zarinpal fee and VAT, as in #1.
